stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .061", Sentence = "However, we found that sport specialization was a positive and statistically significant predictor of child-invested contingent self-esteem (𝛽 = .115, S.E. = 0.047, p = .015) and it predicted higher self-based pride, but this latter effect was not statistically significant (𝛽 = .103, S.E. = 0.055, p = .061)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Parents of children in organized sports have become increasingly involved in their children's sport journeys and there are growing concerns about their behaviors when attending their children's competitions.
One potential driver of these negative behaviors is the inclusion of the child in the parent's self-concept.

In this study, based on the Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP), we examined if levels of excellencism and perfectionism in sports parents were associated with different indices of parental investment in a child's sport, including the inclusion of the child and their child's sport in the self-concept, child-invested contingent selfesteem, self-based pride, and social comparison-based pride.
We recruited 330 parents with a teenager participating in organized sports (Mparents = 43.28 years old; SDparents = 6.48 years).
Results of a confirmatory factor analysis supported the two-factor structure of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) with parents.
Results of multiple regression showed that excellencism positively predicted identification with the child, child-invested contingent self-esteem, self-based pride, and social comparison-based pride.

In contrast, perfectionistic standards were positively associated with inclusion of the child in the self-concept, inclusion of the sport of the child, and child-invested contingent self-esteem, while negatively predicting selfbased pride.
In all, perfection strivers are more identity invested in their child's sport journey compared to excellence strivers.
Overall, the results of the study supported our hypothesis that perfection strivers are at a higher risk of overidentifying with their children who compete in youth sports.

text.formatted: In the MEP, perfectionistic standards are defined as the "tendency to aim and strive toward idealized, flawless, and exceedingly high standards in a relentless manner" <ref type="bibr">(Gaudreau, 2019, p. 200)</ref>, while excellencism is defined as the "tendency to aim and strive toward very high yet attainable standards in an effortful, engaged, and determined yet flexible manner" <ref type="bibr">(Gaudreau, 2019, p. 200)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the MEP proposes a novel bidimensional model of personal standards to shed light on controversies surrounding perfectionistic standards.

Recent MEP research provided a new way to evaluate whether perfectionism is beneficial (i.e., associated with positive consequences over and above excellencism), unneeded (i.e., being unrelated to positive consequences over and above excellencism), or harmful (i.e., associated with negative consequences over and above excellencism; Gaudreau et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent MEP research provided a new way to evaluate whether perfectionism is beneficial (i.e., associated with positive consequences over and above excellencism), unneeded (i.e., being unrelated to positive consequences over and above excellencism), or harmful (i.e., associated with negative consequences over and above excellencism; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gaudreau et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Research in sport has shown that once distinguished from excellencism, perfectionistic standards are associated with tolerance toward cheating and doping in sports (Gaudreau, Boileau, et al., 2025; Gaudreau & Schellenberg, 2022), controlled motivation (Boivin et al., 2025), fear of failure (Gaudreau et al., 2021), lower positive affect (Schellenberg et al., 2026), lower savoring and enjoyment (Gaudreau et al., 2024).

text.text: As for excellencism, it is associated with less positive attitudes toward cheating and doping in sports (Gaudreau, Boileau, et al., 2025; Gaudreau & Schellenberg, 2022) , autonomous motivation (Boivin et al., 2025), subjective sport achievement (Gaudreau et al., 2021), well-being (Schellenberg et al., 2026), savoring and enjoyment (Gaudreau et al., 2024).
text.formatted: As for excellencism, it is associated with less positive attitudes toward cheating and doping in sports <ref type="bibr">(Gaudreau, Boileau, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gaudreau & Schellenberg, 2022)</ref> , autonomous motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Boivin et al., 2025)</ref>, subjective sport achievement <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gaudreau et al., 2021)</ref>, well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Schellenberg et al., 2026)</ref>, savoring and enjoyment <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gaudreau et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, when distinguished from excellencism, there is little evidence to suggest that perfectionism is beneficial.
Perfectionism rather appears unneeded and harmful.
It is common for sport fans to identify with sport objects such as teams, athletes, sports, coaches or even stadiums (Wann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It is common for sport fans to identify with sport objects such as teams, athletes, sports, coaches or even stadiums <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Wann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, little research has been conducted on feeling psychologically connected to an athlete (Wann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Interestingly, little research has been conducted on feeling psychologically connected to an athlete <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Wann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Yet the youth sport context presents itself as an ideal context in which to study this phenomenon.
In recent years, parents of children in organized sports have become increasingly involved in their children's sport (e.g., Bonavolontà et al., 2021; Stefansen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In recent years, parents of children in organized sports have become increasingly involved in their children's sport (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bonavolontà et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Stefansen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: There is also progressively more attention that is directed toward parents in youth sport competitions (e.g., Brodeur et al., 2023; Dorsch et al., 2015; Goldstein & Iso-Ahola, 2008) because they sometimes display inappropriate behaviors on the sidelines.

text.text: Unfortunately, this has a negative influence on the experience of the athletes competing, other spectators, and even officials (Webb & Knight, 2024).
text.formatted: Unfortunately, this has a negative influence on the experience of the athletes competing, other spectators, and even officials <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Webb & Knight, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The way parents behave in the youth sport context probably has a lot to do with how much place their child takes in their self-concept.
More importantly, we believe perfectionism and excellencism may also play a role.
There is some indirect evidence to suggest that perfection strivers may overidentify with their children.

Previous research has found parental perfectionism to be associated with overparenting (e.g., Segrin et al., 2020), transferring one's ambitions onto one's children (Nguyen et al., 2025), psychological control (e.g., Smith et al., 2017), as well as authoritarian and protective parenting, among others (Yıldız et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Previous research has found parental perfectionism to be associated with overparenting (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Segrin et al., 2020)</ref>, transferring one's ambitions onto one's children <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Nguyen et al., 2025)</ref>, psychological control (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Smith et al., 2017)</ref>, as well as authoritarian and protective parenting, among others <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Yıldız et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Parents who engage in such behaviors treat their offspring as an extension of themselves rather than as a separate entity which is an indirect manifestation of overidentification with the child.
Thus, we could expect parents higher in perfectionism to display stronger levels of inclusion of the child in their selfconcept.
As for parents who strive for excellence, they are likely to include their child in their self, but potentially less so than perfection strivers.
Previous research has found that excellence strivers are better than perfection strivers when it comes to balancing different activities at school and in their sport (Gaudreau et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Previous research has found that excellence strivers are better than perfection strivers when it comes to balancing different activities at school and in their sport <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gaudreau et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Other research has found that those who pursue perfection are more likely to make sacrifices that put all their eggs in the same basket for the pursuit of their goals than those who strive for excellence (Pétrin-Pomerleau et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Other research has found that those who pursue perfection are more likely to make sacrifices that put all their eggs in the same basket for the pursuit of their goals than those who strive for excellence <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pétrin-Pomerleau et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These results suggest that excellence strivers are adaptable and that they can make place for multiple objects in their identity and life.
This could make excellence strivers less likely to overidentify with their child.
Research has shown that in close relationships, it is normal and even adaptive to incorporate the other person in one's sense of self (e.g., Aron et al., 1992).
text.formatted: Research has shown that in close relationships, it is normal and even adaptive to incorporate the other person in one's sense of self (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Aron et al., 1992)</ref>.

text.text: This also applies to the parent-child relationship where parents often make their child a part of who they are.
Furthermore, some parents of children in organized sports may also include their child's sport in their self-concept.
However, we believe that identifying with the sport of one's child to a high extent could be an indication of overidentification with the child.
Parents of a child in organized sports are supporters of their child's sport journey rather than competitors themselves.
Therefore, if parents define themselves strongly through their child's sport, they could exaggeratedly identify with their offspring.
Thus, identifying with the sport of one's child could be considered an indirect indicator of overidentification.
We could expect perfection strivers to include their child's sport significantly more in their self-concept compared to excellence strivers.
This would suggest that perfection strivers are at a higher risk of overidentifying with their child.
Research on sport fans has shown that team identification leads some fans to interpret their team's successes and failures as their own (Wann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Research on sport fans has shown that team identification leads some fans to interpret their team's successes and failures as their own <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Wann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, some parents have a tendency to base their self-worth on their offspring's achievement or failures (Wuyts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Similarly, some parents have a tendency to base their self-worth on their offspring's achievement or failures <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Wuyts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Parents with a stronger need to prove that they are worthy as a person may emphasize their child's accomplishments in hopes of being perceived more favorably by others.
This is commonly referred to as child-invested contingent self-esteem (Wuyts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This is commonly referred to as child-invested contingent self-esteem <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Wuyts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This projection of the self into one's child's activities appears particularly relevant for competitive sports where children may be compared to one another based on their performances.
Previous research has found a positive relationship between perfectionistic standards and child-invested contingent self-esteem (Wuyts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Previous research has found a positive relationship between perfectionistic standards and child-invested contingent self-esteem <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Wuyts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Parents higher in perfectionism believe that their child's achievements and failures influence how worthy of a person they are.
However, previous research did not distinguish between perfectionism and excellencism.
It is, thus, necessary to revisit these previous results through the MEP.
On a similar note, it is common for parents to take pride in their children's accomplishments.
Pride has a "highly social nature" in that the triumph of others can "confirm or enhance personal worth" (Lazarus, 1991, p. 271).
text.formatted: Pride has a "highly social nature" in that the triumph of others can "confirm or enhance personal worth" <ref type="bibr">(Lazarus, 1991, p. 271)</ref>.

text.text: In his cognitive-relational theory of emotions, Lazarus (1991) defines the core relational theme of pride as the "enhancement of one's egoidentity by taking credit for a valued object or achievement, either our own or that of someone or group with who we identity".
text.formatted: In his cognitive-relational theory of emotions, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lazarus (1991)</ref> defines the core relational theme of pride as the "enhancement of one's egoidentity by taking credit for a valued object or achievement, either our own or that of someone or group with who we identity".

text.text: Including the child in the self helps explain why parents are often vicariously proud of their child's success.
However, not all parents emphasize the same criteria to define their child's success (e.g., White et al., 1992).
text.formatted: However, not all parents emphasize the same criteria to define their child's success (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">White et al., 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Pride is a goal-congruent positive emotion, highly contingent on what individuals prioritize in their goal system (Lazarus, 1991).
text.formatted: Pride is a goal-congruent positive emotion, highly contingent on what individuals prioritize in their goal system <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lazarus, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: For example, self-based pride results from taking pride in one's child's effort and improvement over time; that is, when they are performing better than they were in the past (Tracy & Robins, 2007).
text.formatted: For example, self-based pride results from taking pride in one's child's effort and improvement over time; that is, when they are performing better than they were in the past <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Tracy & Robins, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: When their child makes effort and improves, excellence strivers could be more likely to be proud than perfection strivers.

Excellencism may be linked to self-based pride because effort and self-improvement are controllable and align with a growth mindset (Gaudreau, Racine, et al., 2025), mastery goals (Chreim et al., 2026), and social development goals (Pétrin-Pomerleau et al., 2025).

text.text: Self-based pride can be more authentic because it raises pride without triggering the quest for power and superiority (e.g., Tracy & Robins, 2007).
text.formatted: Self-based pride can be more authentic because it raises pride without triggering the quest for power and superiority (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tracy & Robins, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, people can experience more hubristic or socially constructed pride when they outperform others (Buechner et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Conversely, people can experience more hubristic or socially constructed pride when they outperform others <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Buechner et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Perfection strivers are hypercompetitive (Gaudreau et al., 2024) and pursue goals through which they want to outperform others (Chreim et al., 2026) and demonstrate their social value (Pétrin-Pomerleau et al., 2025) and superiority (Andrade et al., 2025).

text.text: When their child outperforms other kids, perfection strivers could be more likely to be proud than excellence strivers.
Yet, in sports, the name of the game is winning.

Given that their child is potentially more included in their self, excellence strivers could be more likely to be proud than nonexcellence/nonperfection strivers when their child improves and/or outperforms others in sports.
We had two objectives in this study.
First, we wanted to test the construct validity of the two-factor SCOPE in a sample of sports parents and assess its suitability in this population.

Second, we aimed to assess how excellencism and perfectionism are associated with parental tendencies to overidentify and overly derive a sense of self-worth based on their children engagement in sports.

We selected five identity-related indicators to be investigated alongside excellencism and perfectionism: (a) inclusion of the child in the parents' self, (b) inclusion of the child's sport in the parent's self, (c) child-invested contingent self-esteem, (d) experience of pride when one's child makes effort and improves (i.e., self-based pride), and (e) experience of pride when one's child outperforms other kids in sports (i.e., socially constructed pride).
We had a guiding hypothesis that perfectionism would be associated with indices of overinvestment, but we did not formulate specific hypotheses.
Our goal was to explore how each characteristic of the parents' identity is specifically associated with excellencism and perfectionism.

Consistent with MEP guidelines, the relationship between perfectionism and excellencism is partialled in our regression analyses because both perfection and excellence strivers have high scores on excellencism and both excellence and nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers have low scores on perfectionism (Gaudreau et al., 2024).

text.text: Perfectionistic standards and excellencism were positive and statistically significant predictors of the inclusion of the child in the self-concept.
This indicated that excellence strivers have greater inclusion of the child in the self than nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers.
This also indicated that perfection strivers report significantly more than excellence strivers.
Perfectionistic standards were a positive and statistically significant predictor of the inclusion of the sport of the child in the self, while excellencism was unrelated to it.
This indicated that perfection strivers have made their child's sport a significantly greater part of their sense of self than excellence strivers.
Excellence and nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers did not significantly differ from one another.
Perfectionistic standards and excellencism were a positive and statistically significant predictor of child-invested contingent self-esteem.
This indicated that excellence strivers report significantly more child-invested contingent self-esteem than nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers.
Perfection strivers also reported significantly more contingent self-esteem than excellence strivers.
In addition, excellencism was a positive and statistically significant predictor while perfectionism was a negative and statistically significant predictor of self-based pride.

This indicated that excellence strivers report significantly more self-based pride than nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers, but also that perfection strivers report significantly less than excellence strivers.
Finally, excellencism was a positive and statistically significant predictor of social comparison-based pride while perfectionism was unrelated to it.
Excellence strivers reported significantly more social comparison-based pride than nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers, but do not differ from perfection strivers on this variable.
The MEP is a recent addition to the sport psychology literature.
Past studies found that athletes' personal standards can be differentiated based on whether they focus on excellence or perfection (e.g., Schellenberg et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Past studies found that athletes' personal standards can be differentiated based on whether they focus on excellence or perfection (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Schellenberg et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This study was the first-ever to provide empirical support for the distinction between excellencism and perfectionism in a sample of parents.
A confirmatory factor analysis showed that SCOPE scores fit a two-factor model.
Regression analyses showed that excellencism and perfectionism of parents were differentially linked to their propensity to excessively include their child in their own sense of self.

Overall, these results supported the construct validity of the SCOPE and offered novel insights into the complex ways personal standards can shape how parents incorporate their child into their self-concept.
Results of CFA on the SCOPE (Gaudreau et al., 2022) using dynamic fit cutoffs (McNeish & Wolf, 2023) supported its two-factor structure in a sample of parents.
text.formatted: Results of CFA on the SCOPE <ref type="bibr">(Gaudreau et al., 2022)</ref> using dynamic fit cutoffs <ref type="bibr">(McNeish & Wolf, 2023)</ref> supported its two-factor structure in a sample of parents.

text.text: Particularly, the fit of the model to the data surpassed the dynamic cutoffs tailored to the SCOPE, and the two-factor model fit significantly better than a one-factor model.
This means that parents do observe and understand the distinction between striving for perfection and striving for excellence.

Consistent with previous validation work on the MEP (e.g., Gaudreau et al., 2022), the perfectionism and excellencism subscales were highly and positively correlated and the strength of the latent correlation did not suggest multicollinearity.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous validation work on the MEP (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Gaudreau et al., 2022)</ref>, the perfectionism and excellencism subscales were highly and positively correlated and the strength of the latent correlation did not suggest multicollinearity.

text.text: The internal consistency of the perfectionism and excellencism subscales was excellent.
This is strong support for the construct validity of the SCOPE in parents.

Perfectionism was a positive and statistically significant predictor of the inclusion of the child in the self-concept, meaning that perfection strivers score significantly higher on this variable than excellence strivers.
Taken alone, this finding could be interpreted as perfection strivers being more involved and engaged parents which is considered positive for child development (e.g., Grolnick & Lerner, 2023).
text.formatted: Taken alone, this finding could be interpreted as perfection strivers being more involved and engaged parents which is considered positive for child development (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Grolnick & Lerner, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the positive relationships of perfectionistic standards with inclusion of the sport of their child and child-invested contingent self-esteem outline the need for more cautious interpretation.
Perfection strivers define themselves through their child's sport to a significantly higher extent than excellence strivers.
They also feel as though their self-esteem depends more on their child's successes in sport.
Importantly, the biggest difference found between perfection and excellence strivers in this study was on child-invested contingent self-esteem (d = 0.986, p < .01).
text.formatted: Importantly, the biggest difference found between perfection and excellence strivers in this study was on child-invested contingent self-esteem (d = 0.986, p < .01).

text.text: These findings suggest that perfection strivers excessively incorporate their child into their self-concept.

Further supporting this point, in a supplemental analysis (see Table S3 in the Supplementary Materials), we found that inclusion of the sport of the child into the parent's sense of self explained additional variance in child-invested contingent self-esteem over and above the inclusion of the child in the self.
text.formatted: Further supporting this point, in a supplemental analysis (see Table <ref type="table">S3</ref> in the Supplementary Materials), we found that inclusion of the sport of the child into the parent's sense of self explained additional variance in child-invested contingent self-esteem over and above the inclusion of the child in the self.

text.text: This indicated that parents who identify strongly with both their child and the sport of their child are the ones most likely to base their self-esteem on their child's achievement.
In this study, perfectionistic standards were a positive predictor of both inclusion of the child and the sport of the child.
Perfection strivers were also the ones who reported the highest levels of child-invested contingent self-esteem.
Therefore, based on these results, we can conclude that perfection strivers display some overidentification with their child.

Our results are consistent with previous research which has reported a positive relationship of perfectionistic standards with psychological control (e.g., Smith et al., 2017), parental overprotection (e.g., Segrin et al., 2020), transferring one's own unfulfilled ambitions onto one's child (Nguyen et al., 2025), as well as authoritarian parenting (Yıldız et al., 2020) -variables which are also indicative of overinclusion of the child in the parent's self-concept.

text.text: We found excellencism to be a positive and significant predictor of the inclusion of the child in the parent's self-concept, meaning that excellence strivers score significantly higher on this variable compared to nonexcellence/nonperfection strivers.
This likely means that excellence strivers are more engaged in their relationship with their child (Aron et al., 1992).
text.formatted: This likely means that excellence strivers are more engaged in their relationship with their child <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aron et al., 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, excellence strivers seem better able to maintain clearer self-child boundaries because they do not identify significantly more with the sport of their child than nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers.

Yet excellencism positively predicts child-invested contingent self-esteem, meaning that those who pursue excellence believe that their self-esteem depends more on their child's sport successes than nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers.

Still, the difference between excellence and nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers on child-invested contingent self-esteem is much smaller (d = 0.379, p < .01) than the one between perfection and excellence strivers on this variable (d = 0.986, p < .01).

text.text: Once again, it seems as though excellence strivers can better balance their child in their identity compared to perfection strivers.

The higher child-invested contingent self-esteem in excellence strivers compared to those parents with lower standards might partly reflect the fact that nonperfection/nonexcellence strivers are less achievement driven (Gaudreau, 2019; Gaudreau et al., 2022).

text.text: As potential support for this interpretation, we found that nonexcellence/nonperfection strivers are less likely to experience pride (compared to both excellence and perfection strivers) when their child improves or display effort just as much as when they outperform other kids in sport.
Unfortunately, lower engagement toward the child can have negative consequences for child development (e.g., Grolnick & Lerner, 2023).
text.formatted: Unfortunately, lower engagement toward the child can have negative consequences for child development (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Grolnick & Lerner, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In all, our pattern of results suggests that excellencism reflects a more balanced pattern of investment toward their child compared to perfectionism and non-excellencism/non-perfectionism.
According to Lazarus (1991, p. 272), success is the object of pride rather than its cause.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr">Lazarus (1991, p. 272)</ref>, success is the object of pride rather than its cause.

text.text: As he eloquently pointed out, the fact that "we take credit for success -it is ours and it expands our identity -is the cause, which is what pride is all about".

Observing that excellence strivers are more likely to experience pride than perfection strivers when their child improves and makes effort indicates that defining aspects of their identity were enhanced by the perceived value of their child's achievement.
"In feeling proud we have lived up to or even gained as measured against a personal or social standard to which we aspire" (Lazarus, 1991, p. 272).
text.formatted: "In feeling proud we have lived up to or even gained as measured against a personal or social standard to which we aspire" <ref type="bibr">(Lazarus, 1991, p. 272)</ref>.

text.text: As they value self-based criteria of success, excellence strivers are well positioned to be proud of their child and expand their own sense of worth as they raise an offspring that exhibits goal-congruent values of learning, mastery, growth, and adaptability.
Perfection strivers are less likely to value and expend their identity based on self-based criteria of success.
Contrary to expectations, excellence and perfection strivers did not differ significantly in their propensity to report pride in their children when they outperformed others.
They were both significantly higher than nonexcellence/nonperfection strivers.
In sport, athletes compete against each other and show up with the goal of winning the game.

Winning is ingrained into the fabric of sports, so much that it creates a strong situation in which outperforming others acts as a shared value -a social normamong many sports parents who have a strong need for achievement.
This potential explains why outperforming others is an object that makes both perfection and excellence strivers proud of their child when participating in their sport.
First, the scale we used to assess how much parents include their child or their sport in their self-concept does not clearly distinguish between identification and overidentification.
As a result, we cannot determine the cutoff at which scores reflect overidentification.

Still, we believe our results for inclusion of the sport of the child and child-invested contingent self-esteem provide some support for the idea that perfection strivers overidentify with their child.

Given these issues, we suggest that future research move beyond the quantity of identification and instead examine its quality such as whether it is balanced and flexible or so dominant that it conflicts with important aspects of the parent's identity.
This would be a more direct test of our hypothesis and would require less inferences and extrapolation.
Second, we did not assess behaviors of parents when attending their child's sport competitions.

Although perfectionism is associated with higher levels of inclusion of the child in the self-concept, we do not know if perfectionistic standards are associated with problematic behaviors in parents on the sidelines (e.g., verbal aggression, boasting behaviors, intimidation, etc.).
This should be investigated in future research.

Third, we used a cross-sectional design meaning that we cannot infer that perfectionistic standards or excellencism cause the inclusion of the child or the sport in the parent's selfconcept, child-invested contingent self-esteem, self-based pride, or social comparison-based pride.
Experimental designs that manipulate standards would be necessary to test for such a hypothesis.

In future research, longitudinal designs would be necessary to test for the directionality of the effect, but also to rule the possibility that an unmeasured variable is responsible for the relationships observed in this study.
However, recruiting parents of children in organized sports is both difficult and challenging.
One strength of our study is our large sample size and the composition of the sample which included parents of teenagers competing at all levels of competition.
This strength makes our study a good foundation for future longitudinal work.
Finally, future research might want to replicate our results in young children (i.e., 6 to 9 years old) participating in sports rather than teenagers.
This study was the first to examine excellencism among parents of children involved in organized sports.

CFA supported the two-factor structure of the SCOPE, indicating that the distinction between excellencism and perfectionism applies to parents and extending previous sports studies that focused on athletes (e.g., Schellenberg et al., 2026).
text.formatted: CFA supported the two-factor structure of the SCOPE, indicating that the distinction between excellencism and perfectionism applies to parents and extending previous sports studies that focused on athletes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Schellenberg et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Perfection strivers had a harder time drawing a line between themselves and their child's sport and seemed to overidentify.

Future research should examine whether this makes them more likely to display negative behaviors when attending their child's sport competitions than excellence strivers, who can more neatly separate their sense of self from their child's.
All in all, excellencism rather than perfectionism could be encouraged in parents of children in organized sports.

Complete demographic breakdown of the parents:
Age: The parent's age ranged from 28 to 63 years old (M = 43.28 years old; SD = 6.48).
Gender: Most (63.8%) identified as female and 34.5% identified as male (1.7% missing).

Ethnicity: 78.1% identified as White, 5.4% as Black, 3.1% as South Asian, 2.8% as East Asian, 2.6% as Latin American, 2.3% as Southeast Asian, 2.3% as Mixed, 0.9% as Middle Eastern, 0.6% as Indigenous/Native American in the USA, 0.3% as Indigenous in Canada, and 0.3% as Non-White European (0.3% do not know; 1.1% missing).
Social-economic status: Reported social-economic status ranged from 2 to 10 (M = 5.79, SD = 1.43), 10 being the highest score.

Occupation: Most are full-time employees (65.5%), 18.5% are part-time employees, 7.7% are self-employed, 6.0% are parents at home, 0.6% are unemployed, and 0.3% are university students (0.6% other; 0.9% missing).
Age: The children's age ranged from 7 to 25 years (M = 13.84 years; SD = 2.08 years).
Gender: 60.7% identify as male, 39.0% as female, and 0.3% as non-binary.
Years of competition: They have been competing in their sport for 1 to 12 years (M = 5.08; SD = 2.73).
Hours of practice per week: They practice between 1 and 20 hours of per week (M = 6.08; SD = 4.02) during the competitive season.

Level of competition: They compete at the city level (32.5%), 19.9% compete at the recreational level, 19.2% compete at the regional level, 16.2% compete in inner-cities, 6.8% do so at the provincial/state level, 4.8% at the national level, and 0.6% at the international level.
